aidb_assessment.novelty: Moderate empirical novelty, low algorithmic novelty. The paper openly disclaims novelty in its retrieval algorithms and ridge model. Its distinctive value is the frozen, prediction-first evaluation of marginal evidence-gain routing together with a separate downstream reliability analysis.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The controlled retrieval comparison and explicit separation of retrieval from generation are decision-relevant, and the authors report consequential negative results rather than overstating success. Confidence remains medium because the retrieval events are sparse, utility intervals cross zero, downstream labels are model-assisted, and the public artifacts do not permit complete reproduction.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: Useful as a cautionary and methodological case study. It demonstrates that selective hybrid calls can preserve an observed evidence-hit rate, while showing that this result does not establish answer reliability or real efficiency. It is not yet sufficient evidence for production adoption because human validation, independent benchmarks, and measured costs are missing.

executive_summary: The paper tests a frozen, cost-aware router that chooses between dense retrieval with reranking and hybrid lexical–dense retrieval. On held-out QASPER training-split articles, adaptive routing matches always-hybrid evidence Hit@10 while invoking hybrid retrieval far less often. Neither bootstrap intervals nor provisional answer assessments establish a utility, correctness, or faithfulness advantage. The central validity threat is that answer labels come from a same-family LLM judge with only partial assisted review. Costs are proxies rather than measured latency, energy, or money, and the public repository cannot reproduce all QASPER results end to end. The study supports selective retrieval feasibility and a retrieval–answer-quality disconnect, not improved RAG reliability.

assumptions: The presence of at least one structurally aligned gold evidence unit in the retrieved evidence is an adequate training proxy for marginal retrieval value.
A linear ridge model over six baseline-observable signals can generalize from the sparse rescue and harm examples in development.
The selected unitized hybrid penalty represents a useful routing preference even though it is not calibrated to observed latency, energy, tokens, or money.
Caption text is treated as a retrievable evidence unit even though it may omit the numerical or visual content required by a question.
Provisional model-assisted answer labels are informative enough for exploratory comparison, but not definitive ground truth.
key_components: Keep embeds questions and evidence with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, reranks the leading candidates with ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2, and returns the selected evidence units.
Hybrid combines dense and BM25 rankings through reciprocal rank fusion, uses the same candidate-pool size and cross-encoder reranker, and returns the alternative evidence set.
The policy target is the difference between Hybrid and Keep binary evidence-hit labels, allowing rescue, tie, and harm outcomes rather than a simple baseline-success classification.
Six baseline-only features describe dense-score strength and margin, ranking overlap, movement under reranking, and the share of caption units.
Median imputation, standardization, and ridge regression form the prediction pipeline; a frozen threshold converts predicted incremental benefit into Keep or Hybrid.
Evaluation separates evidence retrieval and proxy utility from generated-answer correctness and faithfulness, with paired article-cluster bootstrap intervals.
method.overview: The authors define Keep as dense retrieval followed by cross-encoder reranking and Hybrid as dense plus BM25 retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion and reranked by the same cross-encoder. A ridge-regression pipeline predicts the realized change in binary evidence Hit@10 from six features computed only from Keep. A threshold, selected with article-grouped development predictions under a unitized hybrid penalty, routes each query. Model and threshold are frozen before held-out gold evaluation. Retrieval policies are then compared on evidence success and proxy utility; outputs from a fixed 4-bit Qwen generator are assessed separately for correctness, faithfulness, and abstention behavior.

open_questions: Would the frozen router retain its evidence-hit and call-rate behavior on the untouched QASPER test set and on an independent scientific-document benchmark?
Would independent blinded human annotators, using a prespecified disagreement protocol, confirm the absence or presence of correctness and faithfulness effects?
How does adaptive routing compare with fixed policies when costs are measured as end-to-end latency, accelerator utilization, energy, and monetary expense?
Would training on evidence completeness, multi-evidence recall, or answer-level utility align routing decisions more closely with generated-answer reliability?
How robust are the policy threshold and coefficients across retrievers, rerankers, generators, context limits, and domains?
What proportion of retrieval and generation errors specifically arises from unavailable figure or table bodies rather than routing quality?

problem.importance: Fixed retrieval can waste computation, while extra candidates may either recover missing evidence or displace useful passages. More importantly, an evidence-retrieval gain may fail to improve the generated answer, so retrieval efficiency and answer reliability require separate evaluation.
problem.scope: The main evaluation is confined to questions about individual scientific articles: both retrieval arms search only units from the question’s source article. The held-out articles come from the official QASPER training split, and generation uses one fixed quantized Qwen model. A separate single-document engineering pilot is diagnostic rather than population-level evidence.
problem.statement: The study asks whether a policy can predict the question-specific marginal evidence benefit of hybrid retrieval from signals available after baseline retrieval, while accounting for the extra action’s cost, and whether such routing improves generated-answer correctness and faithfulness relative to fixed retrieval.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Compare the frozen adaptive policy with always Keep and always Hybrid, without threshold refitting, on the official QASPER test set and one independent scientific-document benchmark.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: The frozen baseline-feature router preserves always-Hybrid evidence performance while reducing measured retrieval cost on genuinely untouched and independently sourced documents.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired difference in evidence Hit@10 together with measured per-question end-to-end retrieval latency; report article-cluster intervals and hybrid-call rate.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop the superiority claim if either benchmark’s interval does not exclude a prespecified unacceptable Hit@10 loss or if measured latency savings fail to exceed the prespecified operational threshold.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Use the published binary-Hit@10 ridge router as the primary baseline, with always Keep and always Hybrid as fixed-policy controls.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Optimizing routing for evidence completeness or answer-level value produces more reliable answers than optimizing binary evidence Hit@10.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Independent blinded-human mean correctness on all paired questions, with unconditional system-level faithfulness that incorporates abstentions.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop if the article-cluster interval for the new router’s correctness gain over the published router includes zero, or if adjudicator agreement falls below a prespecified acceptable level.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Compare caption-only evidence units with a pipeline that exposes extracted table cells and figure content under the same retrieval and generation settings.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Providing actual figure and table content reduces the mismatch between structural retrieval success and answer correctness for visually dependent questions.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Human-scored correctness on a prespecified subset of figure- or table-dependent questions, accompanied by complete-evidence recall.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop if the enhanced representation does not improve both complete-evidence recall and correctness beyond prespecified minimum effects, or if extraction failures make the paired sample insufficient.

However, the public release is explicitly curated rather than a complete experimental archive, so the main QASPER statistics and the diagnostic pilot cannot be regenerated end to end from that repository alone.

results.context: This is the strongest controlled retrieval result. The evidence metric is evaluated on 169 questions, while hybrid-call counts cover all 188 routed questions. Equality on Hit@10 does not mean equivalence has been statistically established.

evidence.quote: Table 1: Held-out evidence retrieval on 169 evaluable questions (60 articles total). Hybrid call counts are over all 188 routed questions.
Utility is unitized Hit@10 minus 0.02 times the hybrid-trigger indicator.
Always Keep 76.92 0 / 188 0.7692 Always Hybrid 78.70 188 / 188 0.7670 Frozen adaptive 78.70 46 / 188 0.7819

results.result: Frozen adaptive routing achieved the same held-out evidence Hit@10 as always Hybrid: 78.70%, compared with 76.92% for always Keep. It used 46 / 188 hybrid calls, versus 188 / 188 for always Hybrid, and its unitized utility was 0.7819.

results.context: The adaptive policy retained the same net increase in successful evidence-hit questions while making substantially fewer hybrid invocations. These counts describe retrieval actions, not total runtime reduction.

evidence.quote: Always-hybrid retrieval yields five potential rescues and two harms relative to keep; the frozen policy realizes four rescues and one harm, giving the same net gain in successful questions.
It selects hybrid on 24.47% of all questions (43/169 among evidence-evaluable questions), thereby avoiding 142 extra hybrid calls relative to always hybrid.

results.result: Always Hybrid produced five potential rescues and two harms relative to Keep; the adaptive policy captured four rescues and one harm. It selected Hybrid on 24.47% of all questions and avoided 142 extra hybrid calls relative to always Hybrid.

results.context: The observed proxy-utility ranking favors adaptive routing, but clustered uncertainty prevents a reliable superiority claim. The intervals also remain conditional on the chosen proxy penalty.
